clinicalPearls: An irreversible obstructive lung disease from fibrosis and narrowing of the small airways (bronchioles)
Presents with progressive breathlessness and dry cough, often with relatively preserved chest radiograph findings
It is distinct from cryptogenic organising pneumonia (the older term bronchiolitis obliterans organising pneumonia causes confusion)
Recognised causes include lung and haematopoietic stem cell transplant rejection, connective tissue disease, inhalational injury and certain infections
Spirometry shows fixed airflow obstruction, and expiratory CT demonstrates mosaic attenuation and air trapping
Treatment aims to halt progression and address the underlying cause, as established fibrosis does not reverse
reference.pathophysiology: Bronchiolitis obliterans is characterised by concentric fibrosis of the submucosa of terminal and respiratory bronchioles, progressively narrowing and obliterating their lumen (constrictive bronchiolitis). An initiating injury, whether immune (as in chronic transplant rejection or connective tissue disease), toxic (inhaled fumes such as diacetyl), or post-infective, triggers airway epithelial damage and a fibroproliferative repair response. The resulting fixed small-airway obstruction increases air trapping and reduces expiratory flow, and because the process is fibrotic it is largely irreversible.
additionalInvestigations: Expiratory high-resolution CT showing mosaic attenuation and air trapping
Assessment for transplant rejection or connective tissue disease
Lung biopsy in selected diagnostically uncertain cases
redFlags: Rapidly declining lung function, especially after transplantation
Features of an underlying connective tissue disease
reference.prognosis: Established disease is generally irreversible and can progress to respiratory failure, though early recognition and treatment of the cause may stabilise lung function; prognosis is worse in post-transplant disease.
pitfalls: Confusing it with organising pneumonia, which is steroid-responsive
Misdiagnosing it as asthma or COPD
Overlooking chronic rejection in a transplant recipient
references: Transplant and occupational lung disease guidelines (standard reference)
management: Identify and remove the underlying cause, including cessation of exposure to inhaled toxins such as diacetyl
Treat the driving process: escalate immunosuppression for chronic lung allograft rejection and use corticosteroids or immunosuppressants for connective-tissue-disease-related disease
Trial azithromycin, which can stabilise lung function in chronic lung allograft dysfunction
Provide supportive care with bronchodilators, supplemental oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, and vaccination
Monitor disease with serial spirometry to detect progression of fixed airflow obstruction
Refer to a specialist respiratory or transplant centre and consider lung transplantation for progressive, refractory disease
